books.section: Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
Truman and the Beginning of the Cold War (1945-1953)

stimulus.source_note: U.S. government photograph of the mushroom cloud over Nagasaki, August 9, 1945, public domain.
stimulus.text: A photograph taken from the air over Nagasaki, Japan, on August 9, 1945, shows a vast mushroom cloud rising above the clouds after the atomic bomb was dropped on the city. The cloud's stem rises from the ground below, and its broad top spreads across the sky.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool: mushroom cloud over Nagasaki, August 9, 1945, public domain (U.S. government photograph)
stem: What did the event shown in this photograph most directly make possible for the United States after World War II?

options.text: A return to the small peacetime army the United States had kept before the war.
options.misconception: The atomic age expanded the military's role; America did not go back to a small peacetime army.

options.text: A new age in which one bomb could destroy a city and shape great-power relations.
An end to all American military spending once the war was over.
options.misconception: The Cold War kept American military spending high long after 1945.

options.text: A decision by the Soviet Union to give up its own weapons programs.
options.misconception: The Soviet Union answered the bomb with a bomb of its own, announced in 1949.

rationales.A: The bomb did the opposite. It made the military more, not less, central, and the United States kept large forces and a huge weapons program.
rationales.B: The bomb that made this cloud destroyed Nagasaki in a single blast. Background from the books: that power turned atomic weapons into the central fact of relations between the great powers for the whole Cold War.
rationales.C: Military spending did not end after the war. The Cold War kept it high, and the arms race pushed it higher.
rationales.D: The Soviet Union did not give up its weapons programs. It built its own atomic bomb and announced it in 1949.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the cloud. One bomb made it, and it towers over the city it struck.
2. Ask what was new. Background from the books: no single weapon had ever destroyed a whole city in an instant before.
3. Ask what that power meant. The country that held the bomb held a weapon no enemy could match, and every great power wanted one.
4. Follow the result. The bomb ended the war with Japan, and it opened a race for atomic weapons that shaped the Cold War.
Remember: the atomic bomb made a single weapon a matter of world politics.
